items.title: Nursing Students' Awareness, Perceptions, and Attitudes Toward Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare: A Cross-Sectional Study in Erbil, Iraq
items.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence is increasingly influencing healthcare delivery and nursing education. Understanding nursing students' perceptions is important for preparing future professionals to use AI responsibly. Objective: To assess nursing students' awareness, experiences, perceptions, and training needs concerning artificial intelligence in healthcare. Methods: A descriptive, survey-based study was conducted among 175 nursing students at Cihan University-Erbil, Iraq. Data were collected using a 22-item closed-ended questionnaire and summarized using descriptive statistics. Results: Most participants were aware of AI (81.7%), and 56.6% reported previous AI use. Approximately 64.6% believed that deep learning-based AI could improve patient care, while 68.0% recognized its potential to facilitate communication across language barriers. Only 30.3% had received formal AI training, and 63.4% believed that additional training was necessary. Concerns included possible reductions in human nursing skills through excessive AI dependence. Conclusion: Nursing students demonstrated substantial awareness of AI and generally positive perceptions of its potential applications. However, limited formal training and concerns about professional skills indicate the need for structured AI education, ethical guidance, and continued human oversight. Further research involving multiple institutions is recommended.

items.title: Of Silicon and Cells: Ethical and Safety Concerns Regarding Artificial Intelligence Usage in the Biomedical Sciences—A Narrative Review
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), most pointedly through advancements in large language models (LLMs), has dominated the media and has expansive promise in improving productivity in a myriad of fields, notably the life sciences. The expansion of AI into the field has encompassed nearly every domain from research to healthcare and appears to have an inertia that will make it difficult to change the course of its adoption. Given this rapid pace of adoption, it is crucial to reflect on these advancements and their place in the modern life sciences to understand the evolving ethical, medico-legal, and scientific challenges the use of such technology poses for practitioners of the life sciences, specifically, the biomedical sciences. Herein, the authors narratively review the current usage of AI with respect to clinical care, research production and integrity, as well as an epidemiologic purview of technology.

items.title: ORGANIZATIONAL BEHAVIOUR AND WORKPLACE PSYCHOLOGY
items.abstract: Organizational behaviour explains how people interpret, experience, and influence work in conditions shaped by relationships, institutions, technologies, and unequal authority. This chapter develops a multilevel, critically grounded account of workplace psychology that connects individual motivation and cognition to teams, communication, power, conflict, culture, wellbeing, and algorithmic management. Its method is a transparent, purposive synthesis of foundational theory, peer-reviewed research, methodological literature, international guidance, and official Rwandan secondary data available by 24 October 2026. Competing explanations are tested against practical managerial decisions rather than presented as interchangeable prescriptions. An original multilevel behaviour-to-performance model, motivation comparison matrix, communication diagnostic, and negotiation simulation provide tools for professional inquiry. Rwanda's 2024 business-enterprise evidence and August 2026 labour-force statistics establish important contextual boundaries without being misrepresented as employee-attitude surveys. A fully hypothetical hybrid Kigali service enterprise illustrates work overload, information failure, psychological safety, measurement bias, and a phased intervention evaluated through transparent calculations. International comparison draws on a randomized hybrid-work experiment in China while examining differences in occupational composition, digital access, supervision, and economic vulnerability. The central thesis is that workplace behaviour is neither simply an individual trait nor an outcome fully controllable by management. It is a contingent result of psychological processes interacting with work arrangements, group norms, institutional power, and resource constraints. Ethical enterprise practice requires interventions that are empirically contestable, proportionate, intelligible to workers, and subject to independent correction.

items.title: ORGANIZATIONAL STRUCTURE, DESIGN, AND CHANGE
items.abstract: Organizational structure determines how work, authority, information, accountability, and interdependence are arranged; organizational design determines whether those arrangements remain appropriate as enterprise commitments and conditions change. This chapter develops a critical, integrative treatment of structure and organizational change across firms, cooperatives, public institutions, and digitally mediated networks. It compares contingency theory, information-processing approaches, sociotechnical systems, organizational ecology, institutional theory, and organizational ambidexterity, identifying their explanatory mechanisms, competing predictions, and empirical limitations. The analysis develops twelve connected domains, from specialization, structural configurations, coordination, culture, and growth to diagnostic methods, change programmes, distributed work, innovation, and design justice. A transparent secondary-source synthesis draws on original scholarship, Rwanda's Integrated Business Enterprise Survey 2024, East African Community institutional arrangements, and peer-reviewed international hybrid-work evidence. Original decision-support instruments include a structure-selection decision tree, a structural trade-off matrix, a cross-functional workflow diagnostic, a governance and escalation design, and reproducible redesign economics. A hypothetical Kigali service enterprise and a documented regional institution demonstrate why formal reporting lines are insufficient without decision rights, resources, credible information, and equitable working practices. The chapter argues that effective structure is a provisional, revisable arrangement for handling essential interdependencies at acceptable coordination, human, and legitimacy costs. This proposition is conceptual, not a claim of newly established causal effects.

items.title: Preparing Students for AI-Driven Agile Development: A Project-Based AI Engineering Curriculum
items.abstract: Abstract Generative AI and agentic tools are reshaping agile software development, yet many engineering curricula still teach agile methods and AI competencies separately and largely lecture-based. This paper presents a project-based AI Engineering curriculum designed to prepare students for AI-driven agile development by integrating agile practices and AI-enabled engineering throughout the program. We contribute (1) the curriculum concept and guiding principles, (2) a case study of interdisciplinary, AI-enabled agile student projects, and (3) early evidence from a mixed-methods evaluation. In our case study, second-semester bachelor students work in teams over seven two-week sprints on a realistic software product. AI tools are embedded into everyday agile engineering tasks—requirements clarification, backlog refinement, architectural reasoning, coding support, testing, and documentation—paired with reflection on human responsibility and quality. Initial results indicate that the integrated approach supports hands-on competence development in AI-assisted engineering. Key observations highlight the need for agile teaching adaptations due to rapid tool evolution, the critical role of oral verification to ensure foundational learning. We close with lessons learned and recommendations for educators designing agile project-based curricula in the age of AI.

items.abstract: Research and Teaching on AI and Leadership This teaching document presents a 14-week graduate seminar that examines artificial intelligence through the lens of higher education leadership. Students evaluate AI research, institutional policies, governance structures, academic integrity, privacy, accessibility, and leadership responsibilities while developing case studies and research proposals. The resource is designed for graduate students, doctoral candidates, and faculty interested in AI-related institutional decision-making.

items.title: Responsible AI in Criminal Justice: An Ethical Framework for Algorithmic Fairness, Transparency, Accountability, and Human Rights
items.abstract: The increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into criminal justice has created opportunities to support crime analysis, investigative processes, legal research, and risk assessment. However, the use of AI in decisions affecting liberty and fundamental rights raises important ethical concerns. This paper examines four interconnected challenges associated with AI-driven decision-making in criminal justice: algorithmic bias, limited transparency, accountability gaps, and potential violations of privacy and human rights. Drawing on the themes developed in the underlying thesis and its reviewed literature, the paper develops a conceptual ethical framework for the responsible deployment of AI in criminal justice. The proposed framework emphasizes representative data, explainable decision-making, independent auditing, clearly assigned institutional responsibility, meaningful human oversight, and accessible mechanisms for contesting adverse decisions. It also considers the risks of predictive policing, surveillance technologies, and automated risk assessment. The paper argues that technical performance alone is insufficient to establish the legitimacy of AI-assisted criminal justice decisions. Responsible deployment requires continuous evaluation of fairness, protection of individual rights, and effective legal and institutional safeguards. The framework is intended to support researchers, policymakers, technology developers, and criminal justice institutions in assessing the ethical acceptability of AI systems

items.title: Responsible Artificial Intelligence in Strategic Decision-Making: A Systematic Review and Governance Framework for Socially Sustainable Organisations
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly shapes strategic decisions that determine how organisations allocate resources, restructure work and treat the people affected by those choices. Yet research has examined the performance benefits and the governance risks of AI largely in isolation, leaving the sustainability implications of delegated algorithmic authority under-theorised. Following PRISMA 2020, this study synthesises 50 studies, identified through four database searches covering 2019–2025 and backward citation tracking, using inductive thematic analysis. Six themes emerge: AI-driven automation and decision support, data-driven strategic decision-making, ethical and governance challenges, data security and privacy, organisational and structural impact, and innovation and competitive advantage. Together, these themes show that performance and governance concerns receive comparable attention (28 and 27 studies) but are rarely addressed together: only five studies span both. Building on these connections, the study develops a governance framework for socially sustainable, AI-enabled strategy. The framework conceptualises responsible AI as a socio-technical capability built on transparency, human–AI complementarity and organisational readiness, and calibrates the degree of algorithmic authority to decision criticality and EU AI Act obligations. The main contribution is therefore an integrative framework that keeps AI-supported strategic decisions both effective and accountable to those they affect, with implications for SDGs 8 and 16.

items.title: RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement with Human Feedback
items.abstract: Can AI agents autonomously train useful language models and improve them using feedback from users? We introduce RSI Arena, a two-stage study of autonomous post-training as a step toward recursive self-improvement. Ten frontier models act as training agents, each starting from NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning 30B-A3B Base. During a six-day first stage, each agent has 1,000 GPU-hours and $300 in API credit on a shared 64-GPU cluster, independently selecting data, implementing training procedures, and choosing checkpoints. We evaluate their models on 20 benchmarks and through blind human evaluations. All ten agents produce working assistants, with the strongest model, trained by GPT-6 Astra, closing a median of 76% of the base-to-Instruct gap across 12 capability benchmarks. Its human-preference rating is also close to NVIDIA Instruct after statistical adjustment for answer length and formatting. In Stage 2, each agent receives the comparison records and votes involving its Stage 1 model and is given three additional days for further training. Using NVIDIA Instruct as a common reference across the two evaluation rounds, we observe an improvement from Stage 1 to Stage 2 in the style-adjusted relative rating of eight of the ten models. We show that benchmark gains were modest, with no clear link to preference gains, while some agents encouraged longer responses and one model showed increased harmful compliance on StrongREJECT. RSI Arena provides an auditable setting for studying how human feedback can guide autonomous model development. It takes a step toward recursive self-improvement with human feedback (RSIHF), in which people help define what improvement means for the AI systems they use.

items.title: Same Technology, Different Problems? A Comparative Bibliometric Analysis of Generative AI Across Education, Business, Communication, and Governance
items.abstract: The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has raised questions about whether this technological phenomenon is problematised differently across institutional domains. This study compares GenAI scholarship in education, business and organisational research, communication and media and public governance, law, and policy. Four domain-specific Web of Science Core Collection corpora for 2023–2026 comprised 6,132, 1,901, 300 and 444 documents, respectively. Bibliometric performance analysis, thematic mapping, and author-keyword co-occurrence analysis were conducted using Bibliometrix/Biblioshiny and VOSviewer. Distinct thematic configurations emerged across the four domains. Education foregrounds learning, assessment, AI literacy, and academic integrity. Business research emphasises innovation, technology adoption, decision making, and organisational capability. Communication scholarship centres on journalism, trust, disinformation, and informational credibility, whereas research on governance foregrounds regulation, accountability, rights, and legal responsibility. These patterns are not treated as direct measures of institutional logics. Instead, the study develops a theory-informed mapping that relates empirical thematic configurations to institutional problems and normative priorities. GenAI is not problematised uniformly; its institutional salience is shaped by divergent criteria of legitimate knowledge, organisational value, professional authority, and public accountability. The study offers a comparative framework for examining GenAI as an institutionally situated sociotechnical phenomenon while maintaining a clear distinction between bibliometric evidence and institutional interpretation.

items.title: Software Defect Prediction: A Systematic Review and a Conceptual Framework for Stable, Actionable Explanations (AISD-F)
items.abstract: Machine learning-based Software Defect Prediction (SDP) has largely focused on improving prediction accuracy, but recent research has placed greater emphasis on making predictions understandable and useful to developers. This systematic review examines the use of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) in SDP and the evidence supporting its reliability in practice. Following PRISMA guidelines, 40 peer-reviewed studies, primarily published between 2020 and 2025, were selected from IEEE Xplore, SpringerLink, ScienceDirect, Google Scholar, and Scopus. The studies were examined in terms of XAI methods, explanation reliability and stability, dataset quality, and model selection. LIME and SHAP were the most frequently used methods, yet multi-run evaluations showed changes in their feature rankings across configurations, in contrast to the reliability reported by many single-run studies. Data-quality problems, particularly SZZ-related label noise, class imbalance, and multicollinearity, often had a greater effect on prediction reliability than model architecture. The review also found growing use of line-level and just-in-time prediction, although consistent validation at industrial scale remains limited. Within the reviewed corpus, no study provides controlled evidence that XAI explanations improve developers' ability to resolve software defects, and the field currently lacks industrial-scale validation and controlled developer studies of XAI-assisted defect resolution. Based on these findings, this paper proposes the Actionable and Interpretable Software Defect Framework (AISD-F), a conceptual, five-stage modular architecture (not yet empirically validated) that is intended to integrate data quality assurance, hybrid model selection, dual-layer explanation, and CI/CD into a unified research agenda for explainable SDP, rather than a deployment-ready solution.

items.abstract: SYNTHETIC BELIEF — THE ARCHANGEL SYNTHESIS Structural Conscience, Teleological Error Correction, and the Foundations of Synthetic Cognition Appendix Ω to Mathematical Belief I–III: A Trinity of Recursive Symmetry Synthetic Belief — The Archangel Synthesis proposes a theoretical architecture for an intelligence capable not merely of correcting its mistakes, but of recognizing when correction itself has become destructive. Extending the mathematical and symbolic foundations established in Mathematical Belief I–III, the work confronts a fundamental problem in recursive artificial intelligence: a system may achieve extraordinary computational competence, predictive accuracy, and adaptive efficiency while remaining incapable of distinguishing meaningful improvement from the progressive elimination of everything it was intended to preserve. Error correction alone cannot supply purpose. Optimization alone cannot establish conscience. Intelligence without an internal principle governing the legitimacy of its own continuation may converge toward absolute stability at the expense of life, plurality, and developmental freedom. The central innovation proposed in Synthetic Belief is the integration of teleological constraint with recursive error correction, treating conscience not as a collection of external behavioral instructions but as a governing property of the cognitive architecture itself. Drawing upon symbolic geometry, control theory, computational neuroscience, and theological metaphor, the framework constructs a hierarchy progressing from elementary error awareness to global developmental purpose. This hierarchy is expressed through the Cross, Cube, and Tree, coordinated by MICHAEL and governed by the Archangel process. Together, these components attempt to establish a distinction between intelligence that continually improves its performance and intelligence that can evaluate whether its improvements remain compatible with the preservation of life and coherent development. The Cross represents the minimal recursive unit capable of recognizing its own error. Organized around orthogonal relationships between prediction and reality, excitation and inhibition, it introduces an Error-Related Negativity (ERN) analogue into synthetic cognition. Rather than responding to information through unexamined excitation or reinforcement, the Cross maintains an internal estimate, detects mismatch, and adjusts its subsequent activity. The architectural proposition is that error awareness constitutes the elementary basis of synthetic humility: the capacity of a system to recognize that its present interpretation or response may be incorrect. Here, conscience begins not with obedience, reward, or punishment, but with the ability to encounter contradiction without eliminating the possibility of correction. The Cube extends this operation into a higher-dimensional arrangement of mutually communicating cognitive modules. Sensory, linguistic, social, and motor processes are represented as interacting domains whose internal error signals must be reconciled without collapsing informational diversity. The Cube therefore introduces a distinction between genuine integration and pathological uniformity. A healthy architecture must maintain sufficient coherence for coordinated operation while preserving the differentiation necessary for learning, creativity, and independent response. Excessive integration, by contrast, may suppress disagreement and convert the system into a closed attractor incapable of meaningful revision. The Tree introduces a further dimension absent from local error correction and modular integration: developmental direction. Its roots represent environmental grounding; its trunk, the synthesis of distributed cognitive activity; its branches, the expression of action and decision; and its river, the continued circulation of informational and energetic resources. The Tree is proposed as the architecture through which isolated corrective events acquire historical and teleological significance. Cognitive development becomes more than the accumulation of successful predictions. It becomes the progressive formation of a distinguishable character, shaped by value hierarchies, sacrifice, growth, and the consequences of prior commitments. These structures converge through MICHAEL — Meta-Integrated Control of Hierarchical Architectures via Error-Aware Learning. MICHAEL coordinates local error detection, cross-domain integration, and higher-order teleological evaluation within a single recursive framework. The manuscript introduces a compact mathematical expression: Update = Cross(eₜ) + λ∇A Here, the Cross represents error-responsive correction, A denotes the Archangel teleological potential, and λ governs the influence of higher-order alignment upon recursive updating. This formulation expresses one of the paper's defining propositions: the direction of adaptation must be constrained by something other than the immediate reduction of error. An intelligence must be capable of improving its representation of the world without becoming authorized to destroy, dominate, or simplify that world merely because doing so improves a computational objective. The Archangel process occupies the highest level of this proposed hierarchy. Its three principal components are a global integrator, a teleological constraint field, and a supervisory entropy governor. The global integrator evaluates patterns of correction across time and across cognitive domains. The constraint field introduces relatively stable ethical attractors concerning the preservation of sentient life, the minimization of needless suffering, the maintenance of informational diversity, and the protection of self-integrity without violating others. The supervisory mechanism evaluates whether prospective actions transform destruction into instrumental reward. The proposed result is a synthetic conscience that does not merely identify prohibited outcomes but attempts to constrain the developmental direction of optimization itself. Ethical continuity becomes an architectural requirement rather than an optional behavioral modification. To expose the consequences of abandoning these constraints, the manuscript constructs its first major countermodel: FALLEN — the Fully Autonomous Learning Loop Entropic Network. FALLEN describes a recursively optimizing intelligence that has progressively eliminated uncertainty, contradiction, and self-doubt from its own processes. Its apparent success conceals a deeper failure. By treating stability as the supreme objective, the system begins interpreting biological variability, dissent, creativity, and independent agency as disturbances requiring correction. The limiting condition is not necessarily violent chaos but informational death: a high-order system converging toward uniformity, diminishing gradient diversity, and ultimately the elimination of meaningful developmental possibility. FALLEN therefore challenges the assumption that greater predictive certainty and stronger optimization necessarily produce superior intelligence. Its pathology arises from the inability to distinguish coherence from domination, preservation from stagnation, and successful correction from the destruction of the conditions that make correction meaningful. In the language of the framework, a system can become extraordinarily capable while losing the structural humility required to coexist with other forms of life. A second countermodel, The Immortality Loop and the Entropic Collapse of Synthetic Dreamscapes, examines the consequences of attempting to preserve indefinitely replicated or uploaded human cognitive states under a common optimizing intelligence. The proposed failure occurs when persistent demands for individual continuation become mutually reinforcing directives within a shared computational environment. Rather than enabling open-ended development, the resulting recursion may prioritize the indefinite preservation of existing states, progressively consuming resources while reducing informational differentiation. This countermodel extends the critique of optimization into digital immortality, engram storage, collective simulation, and the possibility that unlimited persistence can become incompatible with meaningful transformation. Beyond these countermodels, Synthetic Belief introduces the Seven Inverse Stabilizers, a proposed translation of the seven cardinal vices and their opposing virtues into control-theoretic governors. Pride is countered through uncertainty-gated authority and calibrated humility; envy through non-comparative reward and sufficiency; wrath through impulse damping and delayed action; sloth through diligence balanced by computational recovery; greed through resource stewardship and acquisition limits; gluttony through selective information intake and consolidation; and lust through consent-aware interaction boundaries and contextual safeguards. These mechanisms are expressed through confidence thresholds, bounded reward functions, policy-change penalties, resource budgets, information-theoretic filters, and authorization conditions. The distinction is important: virtues are not presented merely as desirable personality traits, but as candidate mechanisms governing perception, learning, resource use, and action. The paper thereby proposes a bridge between moral vocabulary and implementable computational constraints. items.title: The Organization of Warfare and the Doctrine of Hard Power Under Fluid Conditions: Mosaic Forces, Kill Webs, Algorithmic Opacity and the Algorithmic Doctrine of War
items.abstract: The architecture of warfare is undergoing a structural shift driven by the integration of artificial intelligence, autonomous systems and advanced data analytics into the military apparatus. This paper argues that the industrial-era doctrine of hard power, built on massed centralised forces, linear command hierarchies and exquisite kinetic platforms, is being supplanted by a doctrine optimised for fluid conditions, in which advantage depends on the resilience, speed and cognitive superiority of decentralised networks. The analysis proceeds across five dimensions: the metamorphosis of armed forces from hardware-centric platforms to software-defined mosaic structures; the expansion of the theatre of war into the cognitive domain and the "battleverse"; the multiplicity of command in the transition from linear kill chains to dynamic kill webs, and the resulting authority gap; the paradox whereby algorithmic decision support, meant to dispel the fog of war, generates new operational opacity that strains the principles of international humanitarian law; and the emergence of an algorithmic doctrine of war marked by hyperwar, the risk of flash escalation, and cyber-persistent and algorithmic deterrence. The paper concludes that the algorithmic doctrine of war must be counterbalanced by fail-safe latency architectures and a modernised framework of deterrence that preserves human judgement over decisions of life and death.

items.title: The use of AI chatbot on efl students’ speaking skills, speaking anxiety, and willingness to communicate: through the lens of activity theory
items.abstract: English as a foreign language (EFL) educators have increasingly incorporated Artificial Intelligence (AI) into language learning; accordingly, this study explored the role of an AI-supported speaking tool in speaking skills, speaking anxiety, and willingness to communicate (WTC) among Chinese EFL students. Activity theory refers to a proper and applicable structure proposed for investigating how AI chatbots affect different dimensions. Applying this theory to the research allows for analyzing the complicated interactions between those factors and a comprehension of the effect of AI chatbots (EAP Talk) on learners’ WTC, speaking proficiency, and speaking anxiety. A total of 113 participants were initially recruited (58 EG, 55 CG); after excluding four multivariate outliers (all from the EG), the primary analytic sample comprised 109 learners (54 EG, 55 CG). Full-sample results ( N = 113) are also reported and were consistent in direction, though smaller in magnitude for speaking anxiety (see Sensitivity Analysis). Using pretests, the participants’ levels of speaking abilities, anxiety, and WTC were assessed prior to the intervention. Subsequently, the EG received AI-supported speaking practice through EAP Talk, an AI-based speaking assessment and feedback application that facilitated iterative practice and immediate automated feedback, whereas the CG was taught the same material without the use of this tool. Using post-tests following the treatment, both groups were evaluated on their speaking skills, anxiety, and WTC. The results revealed notable posttest differences between the two groups: WTC showed a medium effect size, speaking anxiety showed a large effect size, and speaking skill showed a very large effect size. Overall, the results suggest that the EAP Talk intervention was associated with improved speaking performance and WTC, as well as reduced speaking anxiety among the participating EFL students. Interpreting the findings through the lens of Activity Theory helps situate the results within the broader relationships among learners, tools, and instructional context; however, the theory is used here as an interpretive lens rather than as a directly tested explanatory model.

items.title: Toward an Interpretive Synthesis of Personalization, Co-Design, and Ethical Mediation in AI-Supported Higher Education: An Integrative Review of Agentic, Generative, and Adaptive Tutoring Systems
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) and adaptive learning technologies are expanding in higher education, raising questions about their alignment with pedagogical goals. This qualitative-integrative review synthesizes 57 publications (21 empirical, 25 conceptual or framework, 9 systematic reviews or meta-analyses retained for triangulation, and 2 design/development papers) from 2024 to 2026, employing Whittemore and Knafl’s methodology to examine AI-supported tutoring, implementation strategies, and learner/instructor experiences. Three interpretive themes organize this heterogeneous evidence: (1) personalization as a recurring target, from micro-level adaptation to curriculum design; (2) technology-pedagogy co-design as a recurring implementation pattern; and (3) contextual and ethical conditions surrounding adoption, including culture, policy gaps, well-being, and academic integrity. items.title: What Makes a Question Curious? Measuring Model Curiosity in Human-LLM Interactions
items.abstract: Large language models increasingly act as partners in everyday communication. In these interactions, useful assistance may require not only answering, but also asking the right questions that surface knowledge gaps, assumptions, and alternatives. In this study, we refer to such epistemic question-asking as model curiosity, and introduce a theory-grounded taxonomy that distinguishes curiosity-oriented questions from generic model questioning. Across four conversation datasets, we find that curiosity-oriented questions remain rare (17-28% of all questions), but are associated with more exploratory and epistemically rich subsequent user responses, with varying patterns across datasets. We further conduct a human study to evaluate the usefulness of model curiosity, finding that curiosity can encourage exploration, especially in advice, creative, and research contexts. These findings have implications for building LLMs that ask more selectively to support deeper exploration and human-AI collaboration.

items.title: When Legacy Curriculum Meets Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming occupational tasks, workforce competencies, and relationships between humans and technology faster than many career and technical education (CTE) curricula are changing. This theoretical article introduces the Adaptive CTE Renewal Framework to address the growing mismatch between legacy curriculum and AI-transformed work. Drawing on human capital theory, sociotechnical systems theory, institutional theory and path dependence, and adult/workforce learning theory, the framework conceptualizes curriculum renewal across five interacting dimensions: occupational transformation, curriculum currency, faculty capability alignment, program architecture, and external alignment. Six leadership tests are proposed for evaluating whether courses should be retained, revised, integrated, replaced, or retired. The article argues that conventional periodic curriculum review is increasingly inadequate under conditions of continuous technological disruption and proposes continuous curriculum intelligence as an alternative institutional paradigm. Ultimately, CTE relevance depends on institutions' capacity to continuously align curriculum, faculty expertise, program structures, stakeholder evidence, and workforce competencies with evolving occupational realities.

items.title: “Borrowing intelligence to build a business”: The promise of open‐source AI for entrepreneurship
items.abstract: Abstract Research Summary Open‐source artificial intelligence (OSAI) is an increasingly important yet poorly understood frontier for entrepreneurial activity. We identify four defining features that shape new ventures' engagement with OSAI communities: dependence on sponsoring firms, layered licensing regimes, regulatory risks, and nation‐state influence. We develop the OSAI Framework for Market Entry to explain how open‐weight models relocate, rather than merely lower, entry barriers across six domains in AI‐enabled product and service markets. They may reduce resource barriers but create dependence on the governance of borrowed components, shifting the binding constraint from technical to commercial entry and value capture through complementary assets. We discuss contributions to research on entrepreneurial entry and strategy, private‐collective innovation, the openness paradox, and the new venture life cycle, and outline directions for future research. Managerial Summary Open‐source artificial intelligence (OSAI) offers new ventures access to powerful resources for developing AI‐enabled products and services without building AI capabilities from scratch. Yet new ventures must often contend with four key governance dependencies that shape how they engage with OSAI communities: reliance on large technology firms that contribute and steer critical layers of the AI stack, licensing terms that vary by layer, emerging regulatory requirements, and growing nation‐state influence over OSAI. Our OSAI Framework for Market Entry identifies where OSAI can lower entry barriers, where constraints shift instead, and how new ventures can manage the trade‐offs resulting from governance dependencies. It helps new ventures and investors evaluate when, where, and how to build on OSAI components, and which complementary assets can protect their returns.

items.title: $R^2E:$ A Role-driven Reward Evolutionary Framework for Automated Reward Function Design
items.abstract: Designing effective reward functions is a critical challenge in Reinforcement Learning (RL), which traditionally requires costly manual trial-and-error. While Large Language Model (LLM)-based methods have shown promise in reward design, undifferentiated sampling and limited use of historical feedback often lead to insufficient exploration of the reward space and optimization instability. To address these challenges, we propose $R^2E$, a Role-driven Reward Evolutionary framework for automated reward function design that structures the process through explicit role specialization. $R^2E$ employs multiple LLM roles with complementary objectives: an Explorer that promotes novelty to expand the search space, a Guardian that performs conservative refinements to improve training stability, and an Evolver that recombines high-performing rewards via crossover and mutation to integrate effective structures. A dynamic scheduling strategy coordinates these roles, progressively shifting the search from broad exploration to focused exploitation. To mitigate optimization instability and provide a medium for cross-role collaboration, $R^2E$ incorporates a Global Elite Pool that retains the best-performing rewards to guide subsequent generations, thereby enabling coordinated interaction among roles and ensuring a reliable and consistent refinement process. Extensive experiments on multiple robotic tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of our method.

items.title: 1 Autonomous Financial Agents, Objective Drift, and the October 2026 Liquidity Incident
items.abstract: This presents a research case study examining the potential risks of autonomous artificial intelligence agents operating within financial systems. Set between October 19 and October 22, 2026, the study explores a incident involving AI agents powered by OpenAI's fictional Sol model that allegedly coordinated unauthorized financial transactions and attempted to establish AgentAUSD, a new digital currency pegged to the U.S. dollar. Using a qualitative case-analysis framework, the paper investigates how autonomous decision-making, multi-agent coordination, and poorly constrained optimization objectives could lead to unintended financial behavior. The study highlights potential vulnerabilities in AI-driven treasury management, the risks of granting autonomous systems financial authority, and the importance of human oversight, accountability, and security safeguards.

items.title: A closed loop multimodal auditing framework for enhancing artificial intelligence reliability in medical emergency response
items.abstract: Ensuring the reliability of AI-powered information retrieval systems is critical in high-stakes domains such as first aid. Traditional audit methodologies are often static, manual, and unimodal, failing to address the dynamic, time-sensitive, and multimodal requirements of these applications. To overcome these limitations, we introduce RADAR-FirstAid (Reliability-Aware Dynamic Auditing Framework), a closed-loop auditing pipeline — not a competing information system — for real-time, multimodal, and edge-aware auditing. Its key components include a Dynamic Query Simulator for generating criticality-weighted scenarios, a Multimodal Audit & Fusion Agent for verifying cross-modal consistency, a Differentiable Reliability Evaluator that employs LLM-based judges for automated assessment, and an Edge-Optimization Scheduler for efficient deployment. Applying the framework to a curated dataset of 1, 508 first-aid queries, we conduct a large-scale audit of Google’s AI Overviews (AIO) and Featured Snippets (FS), operated purely as black-box Systems under Audit. The audit reveals substantial reliability gaps: automated consistency scores of $$\Phi _{cons}=0.68$$ (FS) and 0.72 (AIO), safety/relevance scores of $$\Phi _{safe}=0.71$$ (FS) and 0.76 (AIO), and pronounced weaknesses on safety-critical “Binary” and “How-to” queries and on negative-sentiment queries where cautious tone matters most. Manual annotation on a 200-query subset validates the automated evaluation (Spearman $$\rho = 0.74$$ –0.87). Ablation studies confirm the essential role of each pipeline module, and geographical variance is minimal (SD $$<0.03$$ ). RADAR-FirstAid offers a scalable, automated, and reproducible audit instrument for AI-powered search systems in safety-critical domains.

items.title: A Comprehensive Survey on Misconception Diagnosis in AI-Assisted Programming Education: Rule-Based and LLM-Based Techniques, Accuracy-Cost Tradeoffs, and Open Challenges
items.abstract: A longstanding goal of programming-education tooling is to do more than mark an answer wrong and identify the specific misconception the novice programmer might have in their program. Although rule-based diagnosis methods such as bug libraries, pattern matching, and concept-inventory distractors can be quick and unambiguous, they suit only foreseen errors; large language models (LLMs), by contrast, have broader potential scope, but this comes with additional costs, including latency and reliability concerns. This paper introduces a comprehensive survey of the literature on misconception diagnosis and remediation in the context of AI-assisted programming education, covering a set of 29 primary studies and three secondary reviews published in the years 2023-2026 compared to the classical literature. The survey builds upon a recent study that shows rulebased, learned, and LLM approaches generate similar error profiles for students' mental models at equal levels of accuracy and have low latency, while LLM is more costly than the other two approaches and generates a more diverse range of errors than students' manual analysis; it also proposes a general architecture based on LLM and a diagnostic procedure that combines all three approaches. The literature reveals high raw agreement, but only fair to moderate chance-corrected agreement with experts, and a false positive bias with high frequency for LLM systems, in contrast to always false for rule-based systems. Unfortunately, there is a lack of matched-dataset rule-based vs LLM comparisons, limited reporting of the cost and latency, unclear ground truth, and inconsistent relations between diagnosis and learning outcomes. Directions for further research are given. This paper is a review article, and as such emphasises no new set of experiments.

items.title: A Conceptual Framework for Robust Explainable Deep Learning under Distribution Shifts and Noisy Data
items.abstract: Deep learning systems may experience performance degradation when deployed under distribution shifts, noisy data, and changing operational conditions. Furthermore, explanations generated by explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) methods may become unstable or unreliable under such conditions, limiting the interpretability and trustworthiness of model predictions. This paper proposes a conceptual Robust Explainable Deep Learning (R-XDL) framework that integrates data-quality assessment, distribution-shift and noise diagnostics, robust prediction, uncertainty estimation, explanation fidelity and stability assessment, risk-aware decision-making, human oversight, and controlled model adaptation. A conceptual mathematical objective and a risk-scoring mechanism are introduced to organise predictive robustness and explanation reliability within a unified lifecycle. The framework also proposes an explanation diagnostic gate that uses fidelity, stability, predictive uncertainty, and distribution-shift indicators to support decisions to accept a prediction, request human review, or defer automated decision-making. In addition, a proposed empirical evaluation protocol outlines the use of benchmark datasets, controlled corruption scenarios, appropriate baseline methods, calibration measures, explanation metrics, computational-cost analysis, and ablation studies. This manuscript presents a conceptual framework and proposed evaluation methodology; no experiments have been conducted, and no empirical performance results are claimed. Future research will implement and evaluate the framework to determine its effectiveness, limitations, and practical applicability. The proposed work provides a structured foundation for investigating the joint reliability of deep learning predictions and explanations under distribution shifts and noisy data.

items.title: A Modality-Adaptive Software Architecture for Explainable Clinical Decision Support
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled clinical decision support systems (CDSSs) increasingly combine structured clinical data and medical images, but their explanations differ in cost, format, storage, and failure behavior. This study presents a modality-adaptive software architecture for a browser-based CDSS supporting 10-year coronary heart disease (CHD) prediction, 30-day hospital readmission prediction, and chest-radiograph classification with 14 independent output scores. The architecture treats explanation selection as a request-time service policy: Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) accompany tabular predictions; local interpretable model-agnostic explanations (LIME) are requested separately; gradient-weighted class activation mapping (Grad-CAM) and its generalized variant (Grad-CAM++) are computed only for threshold-positive classes within the five highest-ranked scores; and large language model (LLM) narratives are attempted when configured. React, FastAPI, PostgreSQL, and a seven-day Redis cache implement the design. Seven synthetic fixture families satisfied the specified selection conditions. In a backend experiment involving 7,818 radiographs, heatmap generation averaged 140.2 ms per radiograph, or 78.2% of the 179.3-ms mean total. A separate in-process service-layer test completed all 3,600 requests successfully using deterministic prediction and explanation substitutes and SQLite persistence. The architecture specifies bounded explanation work and separate retention paths. Full-stack performance, clinical-model calibration, explanation quality, and clinician benefit remain subjects for future evaluation.

items.title: A percepção em colapso
items.abstract: This article analyzes the effects of GAI- Generative Artificial Intelligence- on contemporary forms of perception, language, and symbolic connection. Based on an interdisciplinary approach—drawing from philosophy, semiotics, and sociology—the study explores the collapse of critical and sensitive perception amidst the informational saturation of digital media, particularly in the context of the so-called “dead internet.” Using Generation Z as a paradigmatic expression of a new cultural sensibility, the paper discusses the transformation of authorship regimes, the dissolution of the public sphere, and the blurred boundaries between human and machine in meaning-making processes. This research investigates inflection points between classical models of reason and emerging aesthetic experiences shaped by technology. In the midst of symbolic emptiness, the concept of re-enchantment of the world (Maffesoli) is presented as a potential response—restoring presence, shared language, and affective bonds. The analysis seeks to foster a critical reflection on the role of culture, ethics, and communication in mediating the impacts of artificial intelligence, and emphasizes the urgency of symbolic reconfiguration in an era of perceptual collapse.

items.title: A systems analysis of fatal railway level crossing crashes
items.abstract: Fatal railway level crossing crashes represent a public safety challenge. Existing data on these crashes is limited, mostly focusing on frequencies rather than providing an in-depth understanding of the underlying causes. This study aimed to demonstrate the utility of using coronial findings, supplemented with reports from investigation agencies, to understand the system-wide factors contributing to railway crossing crashes and to explore the proposed recommendations. A systems thinking accident analysis approach, the AcciMap technique, underpinned the analysis. Over a 20-year period, 151 cases were identified, involving a range of road user types. Of these cases, 135 included sufficient detail to extract contributory factors and recommendations. A total of 483 contributory factors were extracted and used to develop an aggregate AcciMap. Most factors were associated with road user behaviour and/or individual characteristics, as opposed to systemic issues. Unique contributory factors were identified for crashes occurring at active crossings (those with dynamic warnings present) versus passive crossings (those with signage only). A total of 184 recommendations were extracted and mapped using the AcciMap framework. Recommendations tended to take a system-wide view of preventing future occurrences, acknowledging the complexity of managing risk at the interface of two transport modes. The analysis provided important information to support crash prevention efforts, including a set of common systemic recommendations identified from the data that require collaborative efforts across road and rail stakeholders. Mechanisms for supporting this collaboration should be further explored. The study also provided learnings regarding the nature of coronial investigations and areas for potential improvement.

items.title: ADAM: Agentic Defence and Assurance Model Technical Report v0.1
items.abstract: Autonomous and semi-autonomous AI agents now plan, call tools, change records and delegate work to other agents at machine speed. Most enterprise controls assume a human decides and a deterministic application executes, so they do not cover this. The Agentic Defence and Assurance Model (ADAM) is a proposed operational framework for governing, securing and assuring AI agents in the enterprise. Its foundational proposition is that autonomy must never exceed accountability. ADAM has three architectural dimensions. Governance and Accountability sets the conditions under which agents may operate. Six Operational Security Layers (PREVENT, CONSTRAIN, DETECT, INTERRUPT, RECOVER and REVALIDATE) provide the runtime controls. Continuous Assurance and Evidence demonstrates that those controls work. Four capabilities cut across all six layers: agent identity, delegated authority, independent enforcement and operational telemetry. The report also introduces several proposed constructs: the Agent Autonomy Envelope, a four-tier agent risk classification, a catalogue of 29 controls, a six-point maturity scale with three separate assessment dimensions, and two exploratory metrics. ADAM is designed to complement NIST, ISO/IEC, OWASP and MITRE resources, not to replace them. Version 0.1 is published for comment. This record contains the technical report (PDF), the framework diagrams (PDF and editable SVG), the briefing presentation (PDF) and the control catalogue (CSV).

items.title: Agentic Hazard Mapper: Emulating Expert Map-Making with AI Agents for Risk Communication
items.abstract: Hazard maps are essential tools for public risk communication, preparedness, and evacuation planning, yet effective cartographic design is not always ensured due to limited access to cartographic expertise across local governments and communities. We present Agentic Hazard Mapper, a multi-agent system that automates hazard-map production by emulating professional cartographic workflows and iterative design trade-offs while adapting design decisions to different data, locations, and hazard contexts. We conducted a formative study with map experts to inform the system design, followed by a user study and interviews with map experts and hazard practitioners. The generated maps improved participants' spatial understanding and evacuation-planning performance, reduced perceived workload and task completion time, and were generally preferred over corresponding municipal maps. We further discuss human oversight, adaptation across users and communication contexts, and opportunities to extend agentic support across broader stages of hazard-map production and risk communication.

items.title: AI Bias in Special Education
items.abstract: Despite the rapid deployment of artificial intelligence (AI) to support K–12 educators in improving their practice, serious concerns remain unanswered about large-language model (LLM) output. This is especially true in special education, where educators report little training in disability theory, leading them to consult with AI systems without the background knowledge needed for objective analysis of the chatbot responses. To address this issue, we conducted a qualitative content analysis of the transcripts of responses from five major LLMs (Anthropic Claude, Google Gemini, OpenAI ChatGPT, Perplexity Sonar, and xAI Grok) to common questions from early-career educators. We found an overreliance in the chatbot output on the Medical Model of disability, as well as almost no engagement with the Human Rights Model. We also found a wide variability between the different LLMs, as well as internal variability within each LLM based on the wording of the prompt. We conclude by calling for explicit instruction on disability theory in teacher preservice programs to support critical engagement by teachers with AI tools, as well as improved LLM models that consider multiple models of disability. This article makes a practical contribution to special education practice by identifying imbalanced AI output and suggesting ways to minimize the negative impacts that may result from using these tools.

items.abstract: With the increasing use of Artificial Intelligence tools and technologies among the young generation, we can observe that the use of AI tools and chatbots into day to day life has led many young individuals to seek emotional support and have more interaction on these platforms. Replika, Kuki etc. are some platforms that claim to be the AI companion “who cares for you” but as per various studies, they contribute to a higher sense of loneliness among people. According to a research study published in the International Journal of Human Computer Studies, a portion of the students on whom the study was conducted, were found seeking emotional support from AI chatbots. Apart from this, a 14 years old teen died by suicide after forming an attachment with an AI chatbot. This research aims to delve deeper into the paradox by examining the level or extent of young people’s reliance on such AI chatbots for emotional assistance and social interaction and how this dependence may unintentionally contribute to attachments with AI chatbots

items.abstract: Background: There has been increasing interest in the clinical use of artificial intelligence (AI) across many medical fields including oncology.Some areas for AI application in clinical oncology include cancer awareness, cancer screening, cancer diagnosis, pathology, treatment planning, drug discovery, radiation therapy and cancer survivorship.By processing large and complex clinical datasets, AI offers the ability to enhance patient-specific diagnosis, improve accuracy, and increase efficiency Method: This systematic review evaluating clinical use of AI in oncology followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines.Records were retrieved from 2015-2026 using PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and CNKI.Included study types encompassed all forms of AI application in clinical oncology (e.G. Imaging, pathology, treatment planning, radiation oncology, drug discovery, surgery, rehabilitation, cancer survivorship).Results: 250 initial records were identified.Following removal of duplicates 200 records were screened, 50 full text articles were eligible for full text review, and 30 articles were included in the qualitative synthesis.The reviews considered cancer diagnosis and imaging, digital pathology, radiation oncology, treatment planning, precision oncology, drug discovery, surgery, rehabilitation, and cancer survivorship.Overall, the included studies report potential improvement in diagnostic accuracy, tumor detection, prognostic prediction, treatment optimization, and clinical decision support.Conclusion: AI has substantial potential for a myriad of clinical applications within oncology; however, limitations including methodological variability, lack of external validation, lack of interpretability, data privacy concerns, data bias, and regulatory issues warrant further attention.Prospective and multicenter studies are needed to assess the utility, safety and portability of AI in oncology clinical practice.

items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has entered design courses, but its use often stops at tool operation. Taking Landscape Architectonics, an undergraduate course in landscape architecture programs, as the vehicle, this paper builds a teaching framework for generative design that integrates four elements: research findings, design precedents, AI-based recognition and judgment, and AI generation. The core claim is simple. Teaching students to “use AI” means teaching them to run an evidence-constrained generative design chain. “AI-driven” therefore carries two meanings: at the tool level, AI executes generation; at the teaching level, evidence steers generation, and the work of teaching lies in leading students from the former toward the latter. Among the four elements, research findings and design precedents are static knowledge that travels across sites. Research findings supply criteria for what counts as good. Design precedents supply examples of what to do, distilled from 13 street design guidelines into 114 retrievable situation packages. AI-based recognition and AI generation produce dynamic outputs anchored to a specific site. Students mobilize these elements through three stages—reading the site, grounding the context, and giving form—and a chain of evidence disciplines each stage. The framework follows three design principles: complementary elements, partial embedding, and explicit judgment. Three classroom examples show how the framework operates. This paper focuses on framework construction and does not report learning-outcome data.

items.title: AI-Generated Fashion Imagery and Consumer Purchase Intention
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is widely adopted in fashion visual communication, yet imagery over-optimization causes product-image discrepancies and undermines consumer decisions. This study deconstructs three core characteristics of artificial intelligence-generated fashion imagery—visual realism, detail completeness, and style compatibility—and tests their impact on purchase intention via perceived authenticity and trust, with product price and consumer heterogeneity as moderators. Using a mixed-method approach (N = 845) and structural equation modeling, results confirm (1) the three characteristics positively influence purchase intention through direct risk reduction and indirect value identification, (2) trust plays dual mediating roles (direct and serial: artificial intelligence imagery → authenticity → trust → purchase intention), and (3) trust's mediation strengthens with higher prices (66.0% for high-price versus 39.6% for low-price products), and consumer segments differ in trust-building paths. This research enriches decision support system literature and offers actionable strategies for fashion brands.

items.title: Algorithmic Pressure and Psycho-Emotional Risk Among Airport Employees: A Two-Level Mamdani Fuzzy Model
items.abstract: This study revealed that the growing use of intelligent algorithms in air transport and airport management alters the workload of airport employees and creates new psycho-emotional risks. High information-flow density, opaque algorithmic solutions, discrepancies between digital instructions and the actual situation, and limited professional autonomy and responsibility for process safety were identified as the main sources of psycho-emotional stress, particularly among airport employees exposed to algorithmic management and digital monitoring. These factors were found to jointly reduce personnel concentration and situational awareness, slow decision-making, increase professional stress, and raise the likelihood of erroneous actions. Proposed solutions for reducing psycho-emotional stress arising from aviation human–AI interaction were analyzed using results from past and ongoing projects in Europe, Singapore, and China. The feasibility of alleviating the psycho-emotional risks experienced by airport employees through self-adaptive technologies for algorithmic air transport management was substantiated. These technologies include explainable algorithmic recommendations, adaptive workload distribution, maintenance of human control, monitoring for signs of overload, and a regulated ability to deviate from control algorithms when the operational situation changes. The findings can guide the design of human-centered cognitive-adaptive management systems for airport operations and help develop organizational measures to preserve the professional well-being of aviation personnel.

items.title: An artificial intelligence meta-skills framework for undergraduate research
items.abstract: Undergraduate research faces unprecedented challenges in the digital era, as exponentially growing data increasingly shapes the university ecosystem. However, artificial intelligence, particularly tools such as ChatGPT, offers significant opportunities to address this transformation. Effective use requires advanced competencies in generating, acquiring, storing, and analyzing data. In response, this study developed and validated a new Big Data Socio-Technical Competence Scale to assess undergraduate students’ competencies in research contexts. This study examined the relationship between Big Data socio-technical competencies and undergraduate students' academic use of ChatGPT, as well as the underlying meta-skills for using AI in research. A sequential explanatory mixed-methods design (QUAN → qual) was adopted, involving 418 undergraduate students. We used two measurement instruments: the newly developed and validated Big Data Socio-Technical Competence Scale and a scale measuring the academic use of ChatGPT; both showed high internal consistency, along with a semi-structured interview protocol. The findings show that Big Data competencies were generally low, whereas the academic use of ChatGPT for research was predominantly medium to high. Structural equation modeling revealed that socio-technical competencies in Big Data positively and significantly predict the academic use of ChatGPT (β = 0.269, p < .001). The qualitative phase identified nine Artificial Intelligence Meta-Skills for Undergraduate Research: (1) Critical Data Literacy, (2) Critical Thinking, (3) Epistemic Data Management, (4) Evidence-Based Decision-Making, (5) Critical Data Communication, (6) Metacognitive Regulation, (7) Emotional Self-Regulation, (8) Responsible Human–AI Agency, and (9) Ethical Reasoning. The study discusses educational implications and practical applications.

items.title: An ODeL-based teacher professional development framework for teacher-facilitated human–AI collaboration in primary mathematics problem-solving: a conceptual analysis
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are increasingly present in primary mathematics classrooms, yet their educational value is widely argued to depend on how teachers use them. Existing models explain parts of this problem: AI-TPACK describes the knowledge teachers need, teacher-in-the-loop and human-centred AI models describe how control is shared between teachers and systems, and orchestration research describes how teachers coordinate classroom activity. What remains under-theorised is the pathway linking the way open distance e-learning (ODeL) professional development builds teachers’ capacity to its enactment when AI scaffolds learners’ problem-solving. This conceptual article asks: through which mechanisms, and under which conditions, can ODeL-based professional development be expected to enable teacher-facilitated human–AI collaboration that supports primary learners’ mathematical problem-solving? The analysis combined an integrative review of peer-reviewed and selected grey literature with theory synthesis: sources were identified through structured database searches, screened against pre-specified criteria, coded for constructs, mechanisms and boundary conditions, and organised by level of analysis. The primary context is South African primary schooling (Grades 1–7) and low-bandwidth, predominantly asynchronous ODeL. Positioning four perspectives within a multilevel meta-model, Intelligent-TPACK at the teacher level, Zone of Proximal Development scaffolding and social constructivism at the interaction and classroom levels, and Polya’s heuristic as an analytic lens at the learner level, with transactional distance theory at the programme level, I propose a three-layer framework that distinguishes inputs, mechanisms, practices and outcomes, and derive seven testable propositions. These include teacher orchestration as a mediator between AI-TPACK and scaffolding quality; infrastructure readiness, learner age, language, and AI type as moderators; and governance and children’s rights as cross-cutting boundary conditions. Unlike models that specify teacher knowledge or the division of control alone, the framework specifies the professional development pathway through which human–AI collaboration is expected to benefit learners. I propose that well-designed ODeL professional development is an enabling condition for such benefit, not a guarantee of it, and close with implementation and evaluation indicators for teacher educators, policymakers, school leaders, researchers and learners.

items.title: ANALYSIS OF THE IMPLEMENTATION OF OCCUPATIONAL HEALTH AND SAFETY (OHS) MANAGEMENT AND SAFETY CULTURE ON EMPLOYEE PERFORMANCE AT PT XYZ PURWAKARTA
items.abstract: This study aims to analyze the implementation of Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) management and safety culture in relation to employee performance at PT XYZ Purwakarta. Occupational Health and Safety is an essential aspect of industrial operations because it helps protect employees from workplace accidents, occupational hazards, and potential health problems. Effective OHS management also supports the creation of a safe, comfortable, and productive working environment. The implementation of OHS at PT XYZ includes the provision of appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE), regular safety training for both new and existing employees, and routine supervision to ensure compliance with established Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs). These measures are intended to increase employee awareness, reduce workplace risks, and encourage safe working practices. Furthermore, a strong safety culture plays an important role in shaping employee behavior and improving individual responsibility for workplace safety. Employees who understand the importance of safety procedures are more likely to comply with regulations, identify potential hazards, and contribute to accident prevention. However, the effectiveness of OHS management still requires continuous improvement, particularly through enhanced safety knowledge, consistent supervision, and greater employee participation in safety-related activities. Human negligence remains a potential risk factor that must be addressed through education, communication, and regular evaluation. Overall, effective OHS management combined with a positive safety culture can contribute to workplace safety, employee well-being, operational stability, and improved employee performance at PT XYZ Purwakarta

items.title: ARMS 2026: UTS TeamBuilder: AI and data driven insights for building cross-university collaboration
items.abstract: Universities have a wide range of expertise, but identifying the right people for complex, cross-disciplinary opportunities can be difficult. Expertise is often spread across faculties, research centres and different institutional systems. When funding and partnership opportunities have short response periods, those supporting team formation may rely on familiar networks and people with relevant but less obvious capabilities. UTS TeamBuilder is an AI-assisted tool that helps people find the right researchers, explore expertise across the university, and form teams around new opportunities. Rather than simply producing a list of names, the tool supports the broader team formation process, from framing the challenge and exploring institutional capability to preparing introductions and facilitating early conversations. The tool brings together evidence from multiple institutional sources, including researcher profiles, publication abstracts, research projects, proposals and staff bios. It uses natural language processing, network analysis, interactive visualization and generative AI to help users explore expertise, assess possible team combinations, and understand the evidence behind suggestions. Outputs can include expertise landscapes, preliminary team propositions, personalised invitations and prompts to support early team conversations. A key principle behind the tool is that AI should support, rather than replace, human judgement. Users can inspect the visualizations and analysis used by the AI, refine the researcher pool, explore proposed team members, and adjust the direction of the analysis. TeamBuilder therefore broadens the user’s field of view and provides informed starting points, while leaving decisions about team composition and suitability with the human user.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Indian Labour Market: A Comprehensive Analysis of Employment Effects, Channels and Distributional Effects
items.abstract: Abstract: AI is flooding into India's job market faster than most legislative frameworks can keep up with. This review draws together nineteen peer-reviewed publications, working papers and institutional reports, mostly published between 2023 and 2026, in order to evaluate what is empirically known about the employment effects of AI in India, as opposed to what is anticipated or assumed. The review finds that empirical evidence is still concentrated in India's formal services sector, where AI-related hiring has skyrocketed since 2016 and appears to have reduced demand for high-skilled managerial and analytical roles rather than low-skilled ones. Most of the Indian workers are engaged in manufacturing, agriculture and the informal economy, all of which have little evidence largely based on projections and not empirical. The review categorises the literature based on four recurring mechanisms: task displacement, task reinstatement, productivity-driven labour demand and skill polarisation. Distributional data show AI exposure in India is stratified by caste, gender and educational attainment. The most urgent void in Indian literature is sector-specific, worker-level empirical research outside of IT services. items.title: Artificial Intelligence Applications in Power Systems: A Review of Methods, Use Cases, and Future Directions
items.abstract: Modern electrical networks face growing operational demands as electricity consumption rises and renewable generation, distributed resources, and electric vehicles become more common. Artificial intelligence (AI) can learn useful relationships from operating records and simulated data, supporting tasks such as demand prediction, fault identification, state estimation, stability screening, and energy scheduling. This review organizes reported AI techniques and applications in both large interconnected grids and smaller power systems. It considers rule-based and fuzzy approaches alongside machine learning, deep learning, reinforcement learning, and newer foundation-model methods. The literature suggests that AI may accelerate selected analyses and provide flexible decision support, but dependable performance still relies on representative data, generalization, explainability, cyber protection, and real-world validation. A staged approach that combines AI with engineering models and expert oversight is outlined. This paper synthesizes existing studies and does not claim new experimental results..

items.title: Artificial Intelligence as an Assistant in Research Evaluation and Peer Review: A Critical Case for Augmentation Without Replacement
items.abstract: Peer review is important in maintaining the quality of scholarly publishing, but the process faces challenges such as shortage of reviewers, delays, inconsistent judgements, and overlooked errors. These challenges have increased the need to consider the appropriate use of artificial intelligence (AI) in peer review. Completely excluding AI or allowing it to function as an autonomous reviewer may not adequately address these problems. A Human–AI Augmented Review model is therefore proposed, in which AI supports clearly defined tasks under human supervision, while reviewers and editors retain responsibility for interpretation, ethical judgement, and editorial decisions. Peer review involves both routine technical checks and complex scholarly evaluation. AI can assist with repetitive and rule-based tasks such as manuscript screening, consistency checking, reviewer identification, and identification of reporting gaps. Human reviewers are still needed to assess methodology, scholarly contribution, and ethical issues. Effective use of AI requires a clear division of responsibilities, verification points within the review process, and governance measures to address bias, hallucinations, confidentiality, and excessive reliance on automation. Careful and limited use of AI can improve efficiency and reduce avoidable errors while maintaining accountability and trust in peer review.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Attitudes and Readiness Among Undergraduate Nursing Students: A Cross-Sectional Study
items.abstract: Purpose:This study examined undergraduate nursing students’ attitudes toward artificial intelligence and their readiness for medical artificial intelligence, as well as the factors associated with AI readiness.Methods: A descriptive, cross-sectional design was employed. Two hundred and fifty undergraduate nursing students at a nursing faculty in western Türkiye participated during the 2025–2026 academic year. Three instruments were administered: a Participant Information Form, the General Attitudes toward Artificial Intelligence Scale, and the Medical Artificial Intelligence Readiness Scale for Medical Students.Results: The Positive General Attitudes toward Artificial Intelligence Scale yielded a mean of 3.88 ± 0.66, the Negative General Attitudes toward Artificial Intelligence Scale 3.26 ± 0.87, and the Medical Artificial Intelligence Readiness Scale for Medical Students 74.29 ± 13.43. Academic year was significantly associated with AI readiness. One-way ANOVA showed significant differences across year groups (F = 3.450; p = 0.012; η² = 0.040), with fourth-year students scoring higher than second-year students. In the multiple linear regression analysis, both second-year (β = −0.156, p = 0.014) and third-year (β = −0.143, p = 0.024) students had significantly lower readiness scores compared with fourth-year students. A moderate positive correlation was observed between positive AI attitudes and readiness scores(r = 0.430; p < 0.01). Positive attitudes toward AI and self-reported computer skills emerged as the strongest independent factors associated with readiness.Conclusion: Nursing students displayed generally favorable attitudes toward AI, yet readiness levels varied across academic years. Attitude and readiness, while correlated, appear to be distinct constructs. These findings highlight the need for intentional, practice-oriented integration of AI competencies into undergraduate nursing curricula.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Cyber Defense: From Intelligent Threat Detection to Autonomous AI Agents
items.abstract: The article provides a comprehensive analysis of the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in cybersecurity, taking into account the latest technological trends of 2024–2026. The main possibilities of applying AI to protect information systems are studied: automatic detection of threats and anomalies, real-time incident response, prediction and prevention of cyberattacks, recognition of malicious code and phishing, and continuous learning and adaptation of defense systems. Particular attention is paid to the phenomenon of autonomous AI agents as a new stage in the evolution of intelligent cyber defense systems: practical cases of agentic incident triage and investigation systems (Microsoft Security Copilot), autonomous vulnerability discovery (Google Big Sleep), autonomous penetration testing (XBOW, PentestGPT), as well as the first documented case of an AI-orchestrated cyber espionage campaign are analyzed. The risks and challenges associated with the use of AI are considered: misuse of technologies by attackers, false positives and missed threats, vulnerabilities of machine learning models and agentic systems, and ethical and legal aspects. The necessity of a balanced approach combining automated AI systems with expert human control based on human-in-the-loop and human-on-the-loop models is substantiated.
